claims.text: Texas Children’s, Baylor and collaborators announced the BRSK1 study in Houston on September 28.
claims.quote:
HOUSTON (September 28, 2026)
– Researchers at the
Duncan Neurological Research Institute
(Duncan NRI) at Texas Children’s Hospital,
Baylor College of Medicine
, the
Texome Project
and collaborating institutions have identified variants in gene
BRSK1
as a likely diagnosis for individuals with a rare and complex neurodevelopmental disorder who until now had not received an explanation for their condition. The study appears in the
American Journal of Human Genetics.
claims.source_type: primary_institution_news_release Texas Children’s Hospital Baylor College of Medicine
claims.scope_note: September release and research publication; no fresh October discovery.

claims.text: After standard parent-child analyses found no answer, AI-MARRVEL highlighted a rare BRSK1 change as a candidate.
claims.quote:
“Standard genetic analyses of a parent and child with the condition did not reveal an answer, but when a new artificial intelligence-based tool called AI-MARRVEL analyzed the genomic data, it highlighted a rare change in the
BRSK1
gene as a promising candidate for a genetic diagnosis.”
claims.source_type: primary_institution_news_release Texas Children’s Hospital Baylor College of Medicine
claims.scope_note: AI prioritized a candidate; human genetics and experiments supplied additional evidence.

claims.text: Disabling the fly equivalent of BRSK1 caused movement difficulties.
claims.quote:
“We studied the fly equivalent of
BRSK1
, called
sff
(sugar-free frosting), and found that this gene is active primarily in neurons, mirroring the expression pattern seen in humans,” Deng said. “When the fly gene was disabled, the flies developed difficulties moving, showed increased sensitivity to stressors that can trigger seizure-like behavior, became more vulnerable to heat-induced paralysis and lived shorter lives. These findings indicated that the gene is essential for normal nervous system function.”
claims.source_type: primary_institution_news_release Texas Children’s Hospital Baylor College of Medicine
claims.scope_note: sff is a fly ortholog, not the same human gene. Model-organism experiment, no human clinical intervention.

claims.text: The normal human BRSK1 gene largely corrected fly movement problems; patient variants restored function only partially.
claims.quote:
When the researchers introduced the normal human
BRSK1
gene into flies that lack the
sff
gene, the human gene largely corrected the flies’ movement and neurological problems, demonstrating that the human and fly genes perform similar roles. “However, when we introduced the gene variants found in affected individuals, the neurological and movement problems were only partially restored, suggesting that these variants reduce but do not completely eliminate the protein’s activity,” Deng said.
claims.source_type: primary_institution_news_release Texas Children’s Hospital Baylor College of Medicine
claims.scope_note: Rescue means a laboratory fly phenotype, not a patient treatment. Normal gene and patient variants must remain visibly distinct.

claims.text: Additional families reported rare variants in the same gene after GeneMatcher sharing.
claims.quote: “After sharing this finding through a research network called GeneMatcher, additional families reported rare variants in the same gene. Altogether, we studied 10 affected individuals from seven unrelated families,” said first author
claims.source_type: primary_institution_news_release Texas Children’s Hospital Baylor College of Medicine
claims.scope_note: Study families, not general clinical diagnostic accuracy.

claims.text: The paper’s abstract confirms in-vivo fly modeling, locomotor impairment and reference-gene rescue.
claims.quote: We utilized Drosophila to model three missense variants to assess the impact of the variants in vivo. We show that Drosophila sff (sugar-free frosting; ortholog of BRSK1) is expressed in neurons of the larval central nervous system (CNS) and adult brain. Loss of sff leads to viable flies with severe locomotor impairment, bang and heat sensitivity, and a short lifespan. In addition, the third-instar neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) in sff null mutants display a significant overgrowth, associated with elevated levels of Futsch (MAP1B), a microtubule-associated protein. Expression of the human reference BRSK1 cDNA in the sff null mutant rescues the behavioral, NMJ morphology, and Futsch phenotypes, showing that the human gene is functional in flies.
claims.source_type: primary_peer_reviewed_research_abstract NCBI PubMed American Journal of Human Genetics
claims.scope_note: Primary article abstract independently corroborates reported experiments; full article inaccessible in this pass.

claims.text: The paper describes patient-derived alleles as partial loss of function and supports a neurodevelopmental syndrome model.
claims.quote:
In contrast, the three individual-derived alleles (BRSK1
p.Ile202Val
, BRSK1
p.Arg237Cys
, and BRSK1
p.Thr406Ile
) provide only a partial rescue and fail to normalize NMJ morphology and Futsch levels, suggesting that they are partial loss-of-function alleles. In summary, our data support a model that heterozygous loss of BRSK1 leads to a neurodevelopmental syndrome with variable phenotypes.
claims.source_type: primary_peer_reviewed_research_abstract NCBI PubMed American Journal of Human Genetics
claims.scope_note: Three patient-derived missense alleles tested; no general cure, patient recovery or diagnostic performance estimate.

claims.text: Researchers used fruit flies to test effects of gene variants found in patients.
claims.quote:
To determine whether the gene variants in patients disrupt gene function and how, the researchers turned to the laboratory fruit fly,
Drosophila melanogaster
. Fruit flies share many biological pathways with humans and can be used to rapidly test the effects of human genetic variants on the normal functions of specific genes.
claims.source_type: primary_institution_news_release Texas Children’s Hospital Baylor College of Medicine
claims.scope_note: Patient is provenance of the variant, not recipient of the fly intervention.

rejected.claim: Standard genetic analysis came up empty without specifying the tested parent and child
rejected.reason: Initial proposed s2 could generalize failure across standard genetics; source identifies analyses of a parent and child. Revised s2 names this scope.

rejected.claim: That comparison supports a likely diagnosis for families
rejected.reason: Initial proposed s5 did not confine its inference to the studied families. Revised to these families; comparison contributes alongside human genetic evidence.
Release says promising candidate; paper combines genomic identification and experimental evidence. AI alone did not establish causality.

rejected.claim: The fly rescue is a demonstrated human treatment or cure
rejected.reason: Reference-gene and patient-variant rescue occurred in laboratory flies; no patient intervention or treatment outcome reported.

rejected.claim: All patient variants were experimentally tested
rejected.reason: Paper abstract specifies three missense alleles; the human series included other variant types.

rejected.claim: Fresh October discovery, measured diagnostic accuracy, or earlier patient recovery
rejected.reason: Publication and release are September 28. No current October clinical action, diagnostic accuracy metric or patient recovery documented.
DOI redirected to inaccessible Elsevier page; validated primary abstract via NCBI EFetch instead.
